clue.text: Flagpole, first alphabetically west of Mull

parts.note: a flagpole is a staff that a flag flies from

indicators.note: the first letter of the word it picks from

parts.note: A is the first letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: Directions to a flagpole: the first one you meet, alphabetically, lies west of the island of Mull.
explanation.walkthrough: Mull is a large island of the Inner Hebrides off western Scotland; the small island famed for Fingal's Cave lies just to its west.
explanation.definitionFit: The defining phrase locates the island geographically: it is a small basalt isle in the Hebrides lying off Mull's western coast.

clue.text: Might this Asian' be curt with the Sultanate.?

indicators.note: 'Might ... be' suggests the letters of curt could be something else if rearranged

parts.note: Oman is a sultanate on the Arabian peninsula

explanation.surface: A question whether an Asian visitor might behave curtly towards the Sultanate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Might ... be' signals that CURT is reworked into TURC, then OMAN follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: A Turcoman is a member of a Turkic people of Central Asia, so an Asian by origin.

clue.text: How old is the oil. ?. It's vital to a plane

parts.note: fusel oil is a by-product of fermentation, so fusel can stand for the oil
asking how old something is asks its age

explanation.surface: Someone asks the age of the oil, then notes it is vital to an aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How old is the oil?' reads as a question about lubricant; split it as the age of fusel, FUSEL + AGE.
explanation.definitionFit: The fuselage is the main body of an aircraft, carrying crew, passengers and cargo, so it is essential to it.

clue.text: A palace for a Queen.

explanation.surface: A palace has been set aside for a queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Alexandra Palace is a large entertainment venue in north London; Queen Alexandra was the consort of Edward VII.
explanation.definitionFit: One name serves for the London palace called 'Ally Pally' and for Edward VII's Danish-born consort.

clue.text: This nipper was not the pig thief

definitions.text: This nipper was not the pig thief

parts.words: This nipper was not the pig thief
parts.note: a nipper pinches; the nursery rhyme's Tom, the piper's son, stole a pig, but this other Tom from Dickens did not

explanation.surface: A small child is cleared of stealing a pig.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Pinch is the gentle assistant in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit; 'nipper' reads as a child but points to PINCH, and the pig thief is the Tom of the nursery rhyme 'Tom, Tom, the piper's son'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dickens character's surname is a word for a nip, and he is a different Tom from the rhyme's pig stealer.

clue.text: Hobson's choice

parts.note: Thomas Hobson, a Cambridge livery stable keeper, offered customers the horse nearest the door or none

explanation.walkthrough: Hobson was a 17th-century Cambridge carrier whose customers had the horse by the door or no horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hobson's choice is no real choice at all: accept the one thing offered or go without.

clue.text: Vine-dressers' wage-rates

parts.note: in the parable of the labourers in the vineyard (Matthew 20) every worker is paid a penny a day, whatever hours he worked

explanation.surface: A question of what vineyard workers are paid.
explanation.walkthrough: The King James Bible says each labourer in the vineyard 'received every man a penny', so the pay rates are counted in those coins.
explanation.definitionFit: In the biblical parable each vineyard labourer received one coin, a penny, as a day's wage.

clue.text: Bill, the artist about to enquire'the name of the state :

parts.note: neb is an old word for a bird's bill or beak

indicators.note: about means the artist's letters go round the next piece

parts.note: RA stands for Royal Academician, a crossword artist
to enquire is to ask

explanation.surface: Bill and the artist are about to ask what the state is called.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'on the point of', but it puts RA round ASK to make RASKA after NEB.
explanation.definitionFit: Nebraska is a state of the American Midwest, so the clue asks for that state's name.

clue.text: They're'goners

parts.note: goners here means people whose day is gone, whose success is behind them, not people about to die

explanation.walkthrough: 'Goners' suggests the doomed; read it as those whose time has gone.
explanation.definitionFit: People who were once famous or successful but are no longer are said to be past it, their glory gone.

clue.text: The "justice in fair round belly"? No, just a bird

definitions.text: The "justice in fair round belly"? No, just a bird

parts.words: The "justice in fair round belly"? No, just a bird
parts.note: Shakespeare's justice in 'As You Like It' has a fair round belly: a gross beak, since beak is slang for a magistrate; the bird's name sounds the same

explanation.surface: Is this Shakespeare's portly magistrate? No, it is only a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: In 'As You Like It' the fifth age of man is the justice 'in fair round belly with good capon lined'; a fat (gross) magistrate (beak) is a gross beak.
explanation.definitionFit: The grosbeak is a finch with a large heavy bill, its name from French for 'big beak'.

clue.text: A bun is ordered for this jackal-head

indicators.note: ordered means the letters of 'A bun is' are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A bun is ordered for a jackal-headed figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' reads as requested from a menu, but it rearranges A BUN IS.
explanation.definitionFit: Anubis is the Egyptian god of the dead, shown with the head of a jackal.

clue.text: Eye-shadow I prohibit, back in the vegetable garden

parts.note: kohl is a dark powder used to darken the eyelids

indicators.note: back means the words I and prohibit are read in reverse order and letters

parts.note: to bar something is to prohibit it

explanation.surface: Someone bans eye make-up from the vegetable garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns I BAR into RABI to follow KOHL.
explanation.definitionFit: Kohlrabi is a turnip-like cabbage grown as a vegetable, so it is found in a kitchen plot.

clue.text: How a pupil may be expansive in speech?

explanation.surface: Could a schoolchild talk at great length?
explanation.walkthrough: 'pupil' looks like a schoolchild, but it is the opening in the eye, which widens in dim light.
explanation.definitionFit: The eye's pupil widens in the dark, and to speak or write at great length on a subject is the same verb.

clue.text: A doctor among radio comedians finds them pretty bossy

definitions.note: plural noun for an adjective phrase: decorative bosses, pretty things that are bossy

indicators.note: among means A and the doctor are set inside the comedians

parts.note: the Goons were Spike Milligan, Peter Sellers and Harry Secombe of BBC radio's The Goon Show

explanation.surface: A doctor joins a troupe of radio comics and finds them rather domineering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bossy' seems to mean domineering, but it means covered in bosses, the raised ornaments of silverware and moulding. The Goon Show was a 1950s BBC radio comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Ornamental convex flutings on silver or architecture are decorative bosses, so the plural names pretty embossed work.

clue.text: A curious: one alighted here in Rome-of what age?

indicators.note: curious marks the word one as being in an odd, strange arrangement

parts.note: alighted means landed, settled: lit
hic is Latin, the language of Rome, for here

explanation.surface: A strange person landed here in Rome; when was that?
explanation.walkthrough: 'curious' reworks ONE into NEO; 'in Rome' asks for the Latin word.
explanation.definitionFit: Neolithic names the New Stone Age, so it answers the question which period something belongs to.

clue.text: How seldom an engine-strike occurred in Milton's day

definitions.text: How seldom an engine-strike occurred in Milton's day

parts.words: How seldom an engine-strike occurred in Milton's day
parts.note: in Milton's Lycidas 'that two-handed engine at the door stands ready to smite' a single time 'and smite no more'

explanation.surface: Industrial action was rare in the seventeenth century.
explanation.walkthrough: 'engine-strike' suggests industrial action; it is the blow of the two-handed engine in Lycidas, ready to smite 'once, and smite no more'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word for a single time answers how seldom, and it is the very word Milton uses for the engine's blow.

clue.text: A person became a partisan this contest being unfair?

parts.note: one means a person, as in 'one never knows'
to side with someone is to take their part

explanation.surface: Someone took a side, so the contest was not fair.
explanation.definitionFit: A contest heavily weighted to one party is unequal and so not fair.

clue.text: "Where —— low-lieth The breezes pause and die" (Tennyson)

definitions.text: "Where —— low-lieth The breezes pause and die" (Tennyson)

parts.words: "Where —— low-lieth The breezes pause and die" (Tennyson)
parts.note: the missing word in the lines is the name of the woman buried there, title of Tennyson's early poem

explanation.surface: A line from Tennyson with a name left blank for the solver.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's 1830 poem opens 'Where Claribel low-lieth / The breezes pause and die'; the gap takes the poem's title name.
explanation.definitionFit: The blank in the quoted lines is filled by the name of the dead woman in Tennyson's poem of that title.

clue.text: Is middling low after being tight perhaps

definitions.text: Is middling low after being tight perhaps

parts.words: Is middling low after being tight perhaps
parts.note: a rope or wire that was taut droops in the middle once slackened; tight also suggests drunk

explanation.surface: Someone feels only middling and low after a night of drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tight' looks like drunk and 'low' like depressed; read them of a stretched line slackening and dropping at its midpoint.
explanation.definitionFit: A cord droops in the middle when it slackens from being taut, which is the verb for drooping under weight.

clue.text: If you're his friend, say so, or you may be late

definitions.text: If you're his friend, say so, or you may be late

parts.words: If you're his friend, say so, or you may be late
parts.note: a guard calls 'Friend or foe?'; fail to answer 'friend' and you may be shot, the late being the dead

explanation.surface: Advice to declare friendship promptly or risk missing an appointment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'late' suggests unpunctual; it means dead, as in 'the late Mr Smith', the fate of one who ignores a guard's challenge.
explanation.definitionFit: A guard posted on watch challenges anyone approaching and may fire on one who does not answer.

clue.text: Sale gone wrong for American cargo ?

indicators.note: gone wrong means the letters of sale gone are spoilt into a new order

explanation.surface: A sale fails and leaves an American shipment unsold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gone wrong' rearranges SALE GONE; 'cargo' is to be read as 'car go', what makes a car go.
explanation.definitionFit: Gasolene is the American word for petrol, the fuel that makes a car run.

clue.text: Whistles for the Muse'

explanation.surface: Whistling up the goddess of inspiration.
explanation.walkthrough: A calliope is a steam-whistle organ found on fairgrounds and riverboats; Calliope is the Muse of epic poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: One name covers a keyboard instrument of steam whistles and the Greek Muse who presides over epic verse.

clue.text: Sounds very cocky

parts.note: the noise a cockerel makes, and also boastful talk

explanation.definitionFit: A cockerel's call is literally cock-like, and boastful exulting talk is called by the same word.

clue.text: Vicarious discourse ?

parts.note: vicarious read as 'of a vicar': a talk given by a clergyman

explanation.definitionFit: A clergyman's address from the pulpit is the talk a vicar typically gives.

clue.text: Plane sailing

parts.note: the phrase 'plain sailing', meaning easy going, with plane for an aircraft gliding through the air

explanation.definitionFit: Aircraft travelling smoothly through the sky is the business of flying machines.

clue.text: Waterproofin' the film?

parts.note: a grease used to waterproof leather, and with the g dropped, adding a soundtrack to a film

explanation.surface: Someone coats a reel of film to keep the rain off.
explanation.walkthrough: The dropped g in 'Waterproofin'' hints that the answer is a word missing its final g: dubbing a film is adding sound to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Dubbin is grease rubbed into leather boots to keep water out, and also dubbing, re-recording a film's soundtrack, with its g dropped.

clue.text: Maybe it's Nance he's beautifying

definitions.note: a present participle for a third-person verb: the answer means is beautifying

indicators.note: maybe signals that Nance plus he's may become something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: Perhaps it is Nance that he is making look lovely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' rearranges NANCE and HE'S (the apostrophe gives no letter).
explanation.definitionFit: To enhance something is to improve its looks or value, which is making it more attractive.

clue.text: I had turned 51, a man of some refinement, no idler

indicators.note: turned means the contracted form of I had is read backwards

parts.note: I'd is the contraction of I had
LI is 51 in Roman numerals
a gent is a gentleman, a man of some refinement

explanation.surface: Someone who reached fifty-one is a cultured gentleman and still hard-working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' looks like 'reached an age', but it reverses I'D into DI; 51 is LI in Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone industrious and painstaking in work is the opposite of a lazy person.

clue.text: Herring on the doorstep?

parts.note: the Scots street cry for fresh herring, sold door to door, uses a word that also means a visitor at the door

explanation.surface: A fish left on the front step.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caller herrin'' is a Scottish song and street cry for fresh herring, caller being Scots for fresh; a visitor at the door has the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: A visitor who comes to the door shares a name with the Scots word for fresh, used of herring sold door to door.
